newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: San Miguel 1996 net seen down but '97 may recover.
newsitem.headline: San Miguel 1996 net seen down but '97 may recover.

text.p: Higher raw material costs and the burden of funding overseas expansion could cut into San Miguel Corp's 1996 profits, but 1997 may bring more cheerful times, analysts said.

A Reuter poll of seven stock brokerages completed on the weekend showed the food and beverage giant was expected to post a 2.88 percent fall in profits to 5.225 billion pesos in 1996 from a net profit of 5.380 billion pesos in 1995.
Inclusive of one-time gains, San Miguel had a profit of 5.835 billion pesos in 1995.
The firm's 1996 profits were expected to decline despite expectations that sales would rise by about seven percent to 85.088 billion pesos from 79.200 billion in 1995.

"The decline in profits for 1996 will be because of the poor performance of the agriculture sector. It affected San Miguel both on the supply and the demand side. While the cost of their raw materials escalated, the farmers, a main market, did not have enough money to buy (beer)," said Tricia Jocson, analyst at Anscor Hagedorn Securities.
Alexis Cabel, analyst at Angping Securities, said the aggressive overseas expansion by San Miguel in 1996 would cut into its profits.
Helen Alvarez, research director at All Asia Securities, agreed.
"Higher interest expenses brought about by additional borrowings to fund expansion projects in the country and overseas also squeezed their margins," she said.
San Miguel began expanding operations in China and Indonesia in 1996 to make up for a drop in local beer sales, the company has said.

Saturnino Mejia, an analyst at Guoco Securities, the only brokerage firm that projected a rise in San Miguel's 1996 profits, said higher sales in the last quarter and the implementation of a redundancy programme had boosted the company's earnings.
But analysts were unanimous in predicting that 1997 profits would rise. Average numbers from the poll showed expectations that profits this year would rise by about 16 percent to 6.049 billion pesos.
Revenues were seen rising 13 percent to 96.193 billion.

"We project turnaround prospects in 1997 due to the stable price of raw materials this year alongside higher revenues in view of prospects of higher demand for food products," All Asia's Alvarez said.

Alvarez said the government's passing of a law that changed the method of computing beer taxes to specific from ad valorem would also benefit San Miguel. It is widely believed the new tax will affect the company's main rival, the unlisted Asia Breweries.
Jonas Ferrer, research director at Pryce Securities, said San Miguel's overseas expansion may start contributing to the company's bottomline in 1997.
Continued strength of the non-food and beverage business of San Miguel, primarily the packaging segment, will also help boost profits in 1997, Angping's Cabel said.
ING Baring's chief strategist Alex Pomento said: "The recovery in 1997 will be due to a pick up in demand. We are assuming an eight percent overall volume growth in 1997 from zero growth in 1996."
